ex.ko: 이 노선은 배차 간격이 길어서 택시로 갈게요.
ex.en: This route has a long service interval, so I will go by taxi.

배차 간격.nuance: 배차 간격 is not the travel time. It is the gap between one bus or train and the next one.
배차 간격.explanation: 배차 간격 (baecha gangyeok) means "interval between buses or trains". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 배차 간격이 길어요. ("The interval between buses or trains is long."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 배차 간격 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
배차 간격.shortExplanation: 배차 간격 means "interval between buses or trains" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 배차 간격 with 소요 시간. 소요 시간 is how long the trip takes.
Using it for one delayed vehicle. 지연 is delay; 배차 간격 is the normal interval.
Forgetting 이/가 with the measured interval: 배차 간격이 길어요.

usagePhrases.en: The interval between buses or trains is long.
usagePhrases.note: Long interval means more waiting.
Useful with transit apps.

examples.ko: 이 노선은 배차 간격이 길어서 택시로 갈게요.
examples.romanization: i noseoneun baecha gangyeogi gireoseo taeksiro galgeyo.
examples.en: This route has a long service interval, so I will go by taxi.
examples.note: Connects route information to a transport choice.

ex.en: If you miss the last train, you have to take the first train.

막차.nuance: 막차 fuses the native prefix 막- 'last/final' with 차(車) 'vehicle', literally 'the last vehicle', and it dominates Korean nightlife because the subway stops near midnight and missing it means a pricey taxi. Its exact opposite is 첫차 'first vehicle'. Two collocations are everywhere: 막차 끊기다 'the last service is cut off (gone)' and 막차 놓치다 'miss the last one'. The key pitfall is the English verb 'miss' — Korean uses 놓치다 'let slip', NEVER 잃어버리다 'lose (an object)', so 막차를 잃어버렸어요 sounds like you misplaced a train. Also note 막차 시간 is the DEPARTURE time, so a learner who reads it as an arrival time will stroll up just as the doors close.
막차.explanation: 막차 (makcha) = "last train / last bus". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막차를 놓쳤어요. ("I missed the last train.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막차, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
막차.shortExplanation: 막차 means "last train / last bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 막차를 잃어버렸어요 for missing the last train.
잃어버리다 = lose a physical object. Failing to catch a train is 놓치다. → 막차를 놓쳤어요.
Treating 막차 시간 as the arrival time.
It is the departure time of the final train. Arrive a few minutes early or you literally watch it leave.
Saying 막 차 with a space or as 마지막 차 in casual speech.
The fixed word is one token, 막차. 마지막 차 is grammatical but stilted; locals just say 막차.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = to miss (let slip) a vehicle you meant to catch
means its DEPARTURE time, not arrival — leave early

usagePhrases.en: I have to catch the last train.
usagePhrases.note: 아야 하다 = obligation 'must'

usagePhrases.en: The last train is gone (service has ended).
usagePhrases.note: 끊기다 = service is cut off for the night

examples.en: What time is the last train?
examples.note: bare schedule question, the survival phrase

examples.en: Let's hurry before the last train is gone.
examples.note: 기 전에 = 'before ~'; classic end-of-night line

examples.ko: 막차 놓쳐서 결국 택시 타고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: makcha notchyeoseo gyeolguk taeksi tago wasseoyo.
examples.en: I missed the last train, so in the end I came by taxi.
examples.note: 아서 = cause→result; 결국 'in the end' adds the resignation

ex.en: I am going to a senior coworker's housewarming this weekend.

집들이.nuance: 집들이 is a pure native-Korean word (no hanja): 집 'house' + 들이 (from 들이다, 'to bring/take in'), so it literally evokes 'bringing people into the house' — the housewarming party thrown after an 이사 (移徙, moving). Don't confuse the event with the move itself: you do 이사 first (the act of relocating), THEN 집들이 (the celebration). Also distinguish it from 집들이 선물 vs a generic 선물 — the classic gifts are pointed: 휴지 (toilet paper), because it 'unrolls smoothly' (everything in the new home going smoothly), and 세제 (laundry detergent), whose bubbles symbolize prosperity 'bubbling up.' These are warm, traditional choices, not cheap ones — an English speaker may misread practical household items as an awkward gift. It's a relaxed gathering where the host usually cooks or orders in for friends.
집들이.explanation: 집들이 (jipdeuri) means "housewarming party". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 집들이를 하다 ("have a housewarming"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 집들이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
집들이.shortExplanation: 집들이 means "housewarming party" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't read 휴지 or 세제 as a cheap or odd gift — they're traditional, well-wishing choices (smooth unrolling / bubbling prosperity), and bringing them is the thoughtful, expected move.
Don't confuse 집들이 (the party) with 이사 (the act of moving): the sequence is 이사 first, then 집들이. Saying 집들이 when you mean the move itself is wrong.
Don't take the particle 을 for attendance — you 집들이에 가다 (go TO it); 집들이를 하다 is only for the host throwing it.

usagePhrases.note: Said of the host throwing the party
Particle 에 for the event; you attend as a guest
Classic choices: 휴지 (toilet paper) and 세제 (detergent)
The host inviting friends over to the new place

examples.en: There's a housewarming this weekend.
examples.note: Basic 있다 sentence; 집들이 takes the subject marker 가

examples.ko: 집들이에 갈 때 보통 휴지나 세제를 사 가요.
examples.romanization: jipdeurie gal ttae botong hyujina sejereul sa gayo.
examples.en: When going to a housewarming, people usually buy toilet paper or detergent to bring.
examples.note: 사 가다 = 'buy and bring'; these gifts carry traditional good-luck meaning

examples.ko: 이사하고 친구들 불러서 집들이를 했는데 분위기가 정말 좋았어요.
examples.romanization: isahago chingudeul bulleoseo jipdeurireul haenneunde bunwigiga jeongmal joasseoyo.
examples.en: After moving I invited friends over for a housewarming, and the mood was really nice.
examples.note: Real situation; -는데 links the setup to the warm, casual atmosphere of the event

ex.en: People often bring toilet paper as a housewarming gift, you know.

휴지.nuance: 휴지 is the hanja word 休紙 — literally '休 rest/discard + 紙 paper,' i.e. 'paper to be used up and tossed' — and in real life it covers BOTH rolled toilet paper and the flat table tissue you wipe your mouth with; context tells you which. The contrast to learn is 휴지 vs 티슈 vs 화장지: 티슈 is the soft pop-up/pocket pack you carry, 화장지 is the more formal/printed label for toilet roll, and 휴지 is the broad everyday word. Note 휴지통 ('휴지 + bin') means the wastebasket, so don't picture only paper. The pitfall is the particle and the verb: you wipe WITH it, so 휴지로 닦다 (means 로, vowel-final), never 휴지를 닦다 (which would mean wiping the paper itself). Also 휴지 is uncountable-feeling but a torn square is 한 칸 and a roll is 한 통/한 롤.
휴지.explanation: 휴지 (hyuji) = "toilet paper". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 휴지로 닦다 ("to wipe with tissue/toilet paper") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 휴지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
휴지.shortExplanation: 휴지 means "toilet paper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 휴지를 닦아요 to mean 'wipe with tissue'; the tool takes 로 — 휴지로 닦아요.
Don't equate 휴지 only with toilet paper; it also means table tissue. The pocket pack you carry is 티슈.
Don't write 휴지으로; 휴지 ends in a vowel, so it's 휴지로.

usagePhrases.note: 휴지 ends in a vowel → 로; 닦다 = to wipe clean
칸 = a partition/square; the perforated section you tear off

usagePhrases.en: to completely run out of toilet paper
usagePhrases.note: 떨어지다 = run out; the panic phrase in a stall
휴지 + 통(bin); the small trash can, often beside the toilet

examples.en: Please pass me some tissue.
examples.note: simple: 좀 softens the request; 주세요 = please give

examples.en: There's no toilet paper in the restroom.
examples.note: everyday: existence with 없다, subject 가; the stall-emergency line

examples.en: I wiped my mouth with a tissue and threw it in the trash.
examples.note: real-situation: shows 휴지 as table tissue + 휴지통 (bin) in one breath

ex.en: I bought detergent as the housewarming gift, you see.

세제.nuance: 세제 is practical rather than fancy. In 집들이 culture, practical household gifts can feel considerate because they help the new home run smoothly.
세제.explanation: 세제 (seje) = "detergent". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 세제를 사다 ("to buy detergent") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 세제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
세제.shortExplanation: 세제 means "detergent" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 세제 with 세금. 세제 is detergent; 세금 is tax.
Using it for soap in general. Soap is 비누; detergent is 세제.
Forgetting that gift role uses 로: 선물로 세제를 가져가요.

usagePhrases.note: Object marker 를.

usagePhrases.en: to bring detergent as a housewarming gift
usagePhrases.note: 선물로 marks the gift role.

examples.en: It is okay to bring detergent as a housewarming gift.
examples.note: Practical gift sentence.

ex.en: We are the same age, but at first I use polite speech.

동갑.nuance: 동갑 is useful because Korean relationships often adjust around age. Still, being 동갑 does not mean you immediately use 반말; closeness and setting matter too.
동갑.explanation: 동갑 (donggap) = "same age". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 동갑이에요. ("We are the same age.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동갑, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
동갑.shortExplanation: 동갑 means "same age" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 동갑 means you can use 반말 immediately. Ask or wait for the other person to suggest it.
Using 친구 only because someone is the same age. 친구 implies relationship, not just age.
Forgetting final consonant pronunciation: 동갑 sounds like dong-gap, with the final ㅂ pronounced clearly before a vowel.

usagePhrases.note: Common age-discovery sentence.

usagePhrases.en: If we are the same age, can we speak casually?
usagePhrases.note: Age does not automatically remove politeness; you still check.

examples.en: If we are about the same age, can I say we are the same age?
examples.note: Socially careful age question.

ex.en: At first, I tend to call them seonbaenim.

선배.nuance: 선배 (先輩, 'earlier-generation/fellow') means someone senior to you who entered the same school, university, company, or field BEFORE you — a relationship that structures enormous amounts of Korean social life. The sharp contrast: a 선배 is defined by entering EARLIER, while a 상사 is defined by RANK — your 선배 may or may not be your boss, and your boss may not be your 선배 if they transferred in. Also distinguish 선배 from 어른 (an elder/adult by age generally). Unlike 상사, you CAN and do address a 선배 directly, adding 님 for politeness: 선배님. A 선배 traditionally looks after their 후배 (junior), often picking up the meal tab. Register: warm but respectful, deeply tied to hierarchy. The English-speaker pitfall: English has no real equivalent and learners default to 'senior' = 'boss' — but 선배 is about timing, not authority; treating every 선배 as a 상사 (or vice versa) misreads the relationship. Mark whom you learn from with 한테/에게.
선배.explanation: 선배 (seonbae) = "senior (colleague or schoolmate)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회사 선배 ("a senior at work") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 선배, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
선배.shortExplanation: 선배 means "senior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 선배 with 'boss.' A 선배 joined before you but may hold no authority; a boss with power is a 상사.
Confusing 선배 (joined before you) with 후배 (joined after you). They are mirror opposites — get the direction right.
Dropping 님 when speaking TO a senior. To their face it's 선배님; bare 선배 in direct address can sound too casual.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 (company) + 선배 — someone who joined before you, not necessarily your boss.
Add 님 to address a 선배 respectfully to their face.
한테 marks the source you learn FROM; 배우다 = learn.
대학 (university) + 선배 — an older schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: A senior at work helped me a lot.
examples.note: 선배가 + 도와주다 (help, with benefit); past 도와줬어요.

examples.en: Senior, please show me this.
examples.note: Direct address 선배님 + 알려 주세요 (kindly tell/show me).

examples.en: I really respect that senior.
examples.note: 선배를 + 존경하다 (respect); 를 marks the object of respect.

ex.en: Even with a junior, it is good to use polite speech at first.

후배.nuance: 후배 (後輩, 'later-generation/fellow') is the mirror image of 선배: someone who entered the same school, company, or field AFTER you, regardless of their age in some cases (entry timing usually outweighs age). The contrast to keep straight is purely directional — 선배 = earlier, 후배 = later — and neither word is about workplace RANK (that's 상사 vs 부하). Within Korea's senior-junior culture, the 선배 is expected to look after the 후배: guiding them at work, answering questions, and famously treating them to meals or coffee (후배한테 밥 사 주다). Register: friendly and caring, but still hierarchy-aware. The key English-speaker pitfall is honorifics: you do NOT attach 님 to 후배 — 님 elevates seniors, so '후배님' is unnatural; you address a junior by name or with 씨. Many learners over-apply 님 to everyone out of caution, which actually misfires here. Also, don't assume a 후배 is younger or lower-ranked — they're simply LATER to the group.
후배.explanation: 후배 (hubae) means "junior (colleague or schoolmate)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회사 후배 ("a junior at work"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후배 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
후배.shortExplanation: 후배 means "junior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding 님 to 후배 ('후배님'). 님 honors seniors; a junior is addressed by name or with ~씨, not 님.
Mixing up 후배 (joined after you) and 선배 (joined before you). They are exact opposites — direction matters.
Assuming 후배 means 'younger.' It marks LATER entry to the group, not necessarily a younger age.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 + 후배 — someone who joined the company after you.
가르치다 = teach; seniors often guide their 후배.

usagePhrases.en: to treat a junior (buy for them)
usagePhrases.note: 한테 marks the receiver; 사 주다 = buy (for someone's benefit).
대학 + 후배 — a younger schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: I have one junior.
examples.note: 후배가 + 한 명 (one person) + 있다; 명 is the counter for people.

examples.en: I bought my junior a coffee.
examples.note: 후배한테 + 사 주다, past 사 줬어요; the 줬 shows you did it FOR them.

examples.en: That junior is really good at their work.
examples.note: 후배는 + 일을 잘하다 (be good at work).

호칭.nuance: 호칭 is not just a word choice; it signals age, role, closeness, and respect. When unsure, asking 어떤 호칭을 쓰면 될까요? is safer than guessing too casually.
호칭.explanation: 호칭 (hoching) means "form of address / title". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 호칭을 정하다 ("to decide on a title/form of address"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 호칭 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
호칭.shortExplanation: 호칭 means "form of address / title" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an older coworker by first name without checking. Use a title or ask first.
Using 씨 with everyone. It can be neutral, distant, or awkward depending on workplace hierarchy.
Forgetting 님 in respectful titles such as 선배님, 사장님, 교수님.

usagePhrases.en: to decide on a title/form of address
usagePhrases.note: Common after age or role is known.
Safe learner question.

examples.ko: 처음엔 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen seonbaenim gateun hochingeul sseuneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: At first, people tend to use a title like seonbaenim.
examples.note: Polite title choice.

ex.en: If elders are there too, be careful with your tone.

어르신.nuance: 어르신 is respectful and warm. 어른 simply means adult or grown-up; 어르신 adds social respect for age.
어르신.explanation: "elder; older person respectfully" is 어르신 (eoreusin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어르신이 계세요. ("An elder is there."). Watch the particle attached to 어르신 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
어르신.shortExplanation: 어르신 means "elder; older person respectfully" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 어른 when you need respectful tone. 어르신 is safer for elders.
Pairing 어르신 with 있다 in polite speech. Use 계시다: 어르신이 계세요.
Using 반말 around elders just because the setting is casual.

usagePhrases.note: 계시다 is the honorific form of 있다.
께 and 여쭤보다 both add respect.

examples.en: If elders are there too, I will ask, 'May I help?'
examples.note: Respectful presence plus polite help offer.

ex.ko: 눈치 있게 챙기면 분위기가 덜 어색해요.
ex.en: If you take care of things tactfully, the mood is less awkward.

눈치.nuance: 눈치 is a native-Korean word (눈 'eye' + 치) and one of the most essential Korean social concepts: the radar for sensing what others feel and what's appropriate without being told. The distinctions learners trip on are between its set phrases: 눈치가 빠르다 ('quick eye') is high praise, 눈치가 없다 is a real social criticism, 눈치를 보다 means cautiously reading someone's mood (often a boss's, with a slightly self-conscious feel), and 눈치(를) 채다 means to catch on / notice something. So 보다 and 채다 are not interchangeable — one is ongoing wariness, the other is a moment of realization. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 눈치 to 'eyes' or vision because of 눈; it has nothing to do with eyesight and everything to do with social perceptiveness. Living in Korea you'll use and need this word daily.
눈치.explanation: "social awareness, ability to read the room" is 눈치 (nunchi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 눈치가 빠르다 ("to be quick to read situations"). Watch the particle attached to 눈치 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
눈치.shortExplanation: 눈치 means "social awareness, ability to read the room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it as 'eyes' or eyesight because of 눈 — 눈치 is the social skill of reading people, not vision
Confusing 눈치를 보다 (cautiously read someone's mood) with 눈치를 채다 (notice/catch on to something)
Saying 눈치가 좋다 for 'quick-witted' — the set phrase is 눈치가 빠르다; 좋다 sounds off here

usagePhrases.en: to be quick to read situations
usagePhrases.note: 빠르다 (fast) is the highest compliment — your social radar is sharp
없다 (lacking) = can't read the room at all; a genuine criticism

usagePhrases.en: to read someone's mood / walk on eggshells
usagePhrases.note: 보다 (watch) = checking how others feel, often a superior, before acting
채다 = to catch (on); 눈치챘어 = I noticed / I figured it out

examples.en: He's really quick to pick up on things.
examples.note: 눈치 빠르다 drops 가 in casual speech; the go-to banmal compliment for social sharpness

examples.ko: 저는 눈치가 없어서 분위기를 잘 못 읽어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun nunchiga eopseoseo bunwigireul jal mot ilgeoyo.
examples.en: I'm a bit clueless, so I don't read the mood well.
examples.note: 분위기를 읽다 = read the atmosphere; a humble self-description in polite speech

examples.ko: 사장님 눈치 보느라 일찍 못 가요.
examples.romanization: sajangnim nunchi boneura iljjing mot gayo.
examples.en: I can't leave early because I'm watching the boss's mood.
examples.note: -느라 = on account of (doing); 눈치 보다 toward a superior is classic office reality

ex.en: It is a little awkward because it is the first meeting.

어색하다.nuance: 어색하다 traces to the Sino-Korean 語塞 (어 語 'speech' + 색 塞 'blocked/stuck') — the picture of words getting jammed — and names two feelings: the stiff, uneasy awkwardness between people who aren't yet close, and the sense that something looks or feels unnatural or out of place (a forced smile, a new haircut, an odd-sounding sentence). It is the antonym of 자연스럽다 (natural). Draw the line from 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: those are shyness/embarrassment about YOURSELF (blushing, shame), whereas 어색하다 is the awkwardness of an unfamiliar situation or relationship — no shame, just lack of ease; and 불편하다 is broader discomfort, while 어색하다 specifically flags social unfamiliarity. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 어색해요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 어색하다 for personal embarrassment ('I was so embarrassed' is 창피했어요); reserve 어색하다 for that not-yet-comfortable-together or 'this looks unnatural' feeling.
어색하다.explanation: 어색하다 (eosaekada) means "to be awkward; unnatural". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어색해요 ("It's awkward"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 어색하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
어색하다.shortExplanation: 어색하다 means "to be awkward; unnatural" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 부끄럽다/창피하다 (shy/embarrassed) — 어색하다 is awkward unfamiliarity, not personal shame.
Conjugating as 어색하요; 하다 adjectives become 어색해요.
Treating it as a synonym of 불편하다 — 어색하다 is narrower: specifically the social awkwardness of not being close yet.

도와드리다.nuance: 도와드리다 is the humble form of 도와주다 ('help (as a favour)'), where 돕다 (to help) becomes 도와- by the ㅂ-irregular (돕 + 아 → 도와), and the helper-benefit 주다 is upgraded to its humble twin 드리다. So it literally means 'humbly do the favour of helping' — you lower yourself to help someone above you: a customer, elder, or guest. Contrast the three levels you must keep straight: 돕다 (bare dictionary 'help'), 도와주다 (help someone, neutral/friendly), 도와드리다 (help a superior, humble). English flattens all of these to 'help', so the pitfall is using 도와주다 with a customer (too casual for service) or, conversely, 도와드리다 with a buddy (oddly stiff). The phrase 무엇을 도와드릴까요? is the fixed, must-know service line. Conjugation follows 드리다: 도와드려요, 도와드렸어요.
도와드리다.explanation: 도와드리다 (dowadeurida) means "to help (politely)". Start from the polite form 도와드려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 도와드리다. A strong first sentence is 무엇을 도와드릴까요? ("How may I help you?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 도와드리다 also becomes 도와드리고 싶어요 (want), 도와드릴 수 있어요 (can), and 못 도와드려요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
도와드리다.shortExplanation: 도와드리다 means "to help (politely)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 도와드리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 도와드려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 도와줄까요? to a customer or elder — it's too casual for service; the polite form is 도와드릴까요?.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular and writing 돕아드려요; 돕다 + 아 becomes 도와-, so it's 도와드려요.
Using 도와드리다 toward a younger friend; among peers 도와줄게 (도와주다) is natural and 도와드릴게 sounds over-formal.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 도와드리다 becomes 도와드릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 도와드릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 도와드리다 has an irregular stem (ㅂ irregular (돕다)). Memorize its polite form 도와드려요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

수고하셨습니다.en: thank you for your hard work

ex.en: Thank you for inviting me today. Thank you for your hard work.

수고하셨습니다.nuance: 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges finished effort. 수고(受苦 / loosely) means 'trouble, effort, hard work'; 하시— is the honorific stem of 하다 'to do'; and the past -셨- marks completion, so the phrase means '(you) have done hard work'. The make-or-break contrast is TENSE and DIRECTION. Tense: 수고하셨습니다 (past, work is finished) vs 수고하세요 (present, person is still at it — used as you leave). Mix these and you are either congratulating someone mid-task or urging a finished person to keep going. Direction: 수고하셨습니다 flows naturally downward (superior to junior) or sideways (peers), but upward to a clearly senior boss it can sound presumptuous, as if you are evaluating their effort from a position of authority you don't have — to a superior, 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 is safer. The near-synonym 고생하셨습니다 (고생 'hardship/toil') feels warmer and more empathetic about the difficulty of the work, not just the fact of effort. Casual register: 수고했어 (반말, to a junior or close peer). The English-speaker pitfall is conflating it with a casual 'thanks' and dropping it on anyone regardless of rank or whether the work is done.
수고하셨습니다.explanation: "Thank you for your hard work." — that is 수고하셨습니다 (sugohasyeotseumnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 수고하셨습니다 ("thank you for your hard work"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
수고하셨습니다.shortExplanation: 수고하셨습니다 is a practical expression meaning "Thank you for your hard work.".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 수고하셨습니다 upward to a clearly higher-ranking boss — directed upward it can sound presumptuous, as if you are evaluating their effort; to a superior use 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 with care.
Confusing the tenses — 수고하셨습니다 is for FINISHED work; if the person is still working, the present-tense 수고하세요 is the correct phrase.
Using casual 반말 수고했어 with someone you owe politeness to — that form is only for juniors or close peers; otherwise keep 수고하셨습니다 or at least 수고하셨어요.

usagePhrases.en: thank you for your hard work
usagePhrases.note: formal (합쇼체 + honorific) — after completed work, best from a superior or peer, not directed upward
softer polite version (해요체) — same situation, slightly less formal
present tense — to someone STILL working as you depart; this is NOT the same phrase as 하셨습니다

usagePhrases.en: thank you for all your hard effort
usagePhrases.note: warmer near-synonym — 고생 ('hardship/toil') feels more heartfelt about the difficulty endured than 수고

examples.ko: A: 발표 정말 수고하셨습니다. 덕분에 잘 됐어요. / B: 감사합니다. 열심히 준비했습니다.
examples.romanization: A: balpyo jeongmal sugohasyeotseumnida. deokbune jal dwaesseoyo. / B: gamsahamnida. yeolsimhi junbihaetseumnida.
examples.en: A: You really worked hard on that presentation. It went great thanks to you. / B: Thank you. I prepared hard for it.
examples.note: supervisor (A) thanks the presenter (B) after the presentation — 수고하셨습니다 flows naturally downward from A to B after completed work

examples.en: Thank you for your work in today's meeting. See you tomorrow.
examples.note: wrapping up a meeting — 수고하셨습니다 marks the task as finished; pairs with the next-meeting farewell

examples.ko: A: 다들 수고하세요. 저 먼저 퇴근합니다. / B: 네, 안녕히 가세요.
examples.romanization: A: dadeul sugohaseyo. jeo meonjeo toegeunhamnida. / B: ne, annyeonghi gaseyo.
examples.en: A: Everyone, keep at it. I'm heading home first. / B: Yes, take care. Goodbye.
examples.note: present-tense 수고하세요 directed at colleagues who are still working — notice the tense difference from 하셨습니다

ex.en: Thanks to you, the atmosphere became comfortable.

덕분에.nuance: 덕분에 is for welcome causes. 때문에 often sounds neutral or negative, so 선배님 때문에 잘 됐어요 can sound like blame even with a good result.
덕분에.explanation: 덕분에 (deokbune) means "thanks to". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 선배님 덕분에 ("thanks to you / thanks to the senior colleague"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 덕분에 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
덕분에.shortExplanation: 덕분에 means "thanks to" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 때문에 to thank someone. Use 덕분에 for a positive cause.
Forgetting the person before 덕분에: 선배님 덕분에, 친구 덕분에.
Using 덕분에 for a bad result. For bad results, 때문에 is usually natural.

usagePhrases.en: It went well thanks to you.
